page: Amazon Web Services r5d.16xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the Nitro hypervisor. It features an Intel Xeon 8259CL x86_64 processor running at 3.1 GHz, delivering 64 vCPUs across 32 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The system is equipped with 512.0 GB of DDR4 memory operating at 3 GHz, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per physical core. Local storage is bundled as a 2400 GB NVMe SSD, and baseline network bandwidth is rated at 20 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates a clear performance tradeoff between single-core and multi-core operations. Single-core CPU performance is weak, as shown by stress-ng single-core and Geekbench single-core scores falling into the bottom 25%. However, multi-core performance is average, with the 64 vCPUs delivering middle-tier results in stress-ng multi-core, Passmark CPU, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression. Memory performance is a notable strength, with large-block read-only and write memory bandwidth benchmarks ranking in the top 25%, reaching 209.41 GB/sec and 92.36 GB/sec respectively.

This instance type offers high resource density by combining a large memory footprint with fast local NVMe storage, making it qualitatively cost-efficient for workloads that require high memory capacity and low-latency local scratch space. It is suited for database operations, as reflected in its average Passmark database and Redis SET performance. Other appropriate workloads include memory-intensive data processing, static web serving, and multi-threaded software compilation, whereas single-threaded tasks and large LLM text generation are limited by the weaker single-core CPU capabilities.
description: Amazon Web Services r5d.16xlarge is a memory-optimized instance featuring 64 vCPUs and 32 physical cores powered by an Intel Xeon 8259CL x86_64 processor running at 3.1 GHz. It is equipped with 512.0 GB of DDR4 RAM and 2400 GB of local NVMe SSD storage, operating on the Nitro hypervisor with a 20 Gbps baseline network speed. Benchmark results show a distinct tradeoff: single-core CPU performance and single-threaded compression tasks fall into the bottom 25%, while multi-core performance and database operations remain in the average tier. Notably, large-block memory bandwidth is strong, placing in the top 25% with read speeds of 209.41 GB/sec. This hardware profile is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-intensive and storage-heavy workloads, making it suitable for database deployments, Redis caching, and multi-threaded data processing rather than single-threaded or compute-heavy tasks.
